content: The TNNI1 gene encodes the protein Troponin I, slow skeletal muscle, in humans. This protein is a tissue-specific subtype of Troponin I, which is a component of the troponin complex. The TNNI1 gene is located on human chromosome 3 and encodes the slow-twitch skeletal muscle isoform of Troponin I (ssTnI), which serves as the inhibitory subunit of the troponin complex in striated muscle myofilaments. The gene spans approximately 5 kilobases of genomic DNA and consists of 9 exons and 8 introns. Gene Evolution Three homologous genes have evolved in vertebrates, encoding three muscle type-specific isoforms of Troponin I. In mammals, the amino acid sequence of ssTnI is highly conserved. Mouse and bovine ssTnI differ from human ssTnI by only four amino acids, while rhesus monkey ssTnI is identical to the human sequence. In lower vertebrates, the divergence of ssTnI between species is greater than that observed in higher vertebrates. Tissue Distribution Compared to the fast-twitch skeletal muscle and cardiac Troponin I isoform genes (TNNI2 and TNNI3), TNNI1 exhibits a broader range of expression in avian and mammalian striated muscles. It is the predominant Troponin I isoform expressed in both slow skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle during early embryonic stages. During perinatal heart development, an isoform switch occurs from ssTnI to cardiac Troponin I (cTnI). In contrast, ssTnI is not expressed in the embryonic hearts of Xenopus and zebrafish but is expressed in somites and skeletal muscles. Structure-Function Relationships The primary function of Troponin I is to regulate striated muscle contraction and relaxation. Troponin I interacts with all major regulatory proteins in the sarcomeric thin filaments of cardiac and skeletal muscles, including Troponin C, Troponin T, tropomyosin, and actin. When cytosolic calcium (Ca²⁺) levels are low, Troponin I binds to the thin filament, blocking the myosin-binding sites on actin. An increase in cytosolic Ca²⁺ leads to calcium binding to the N-terminal domain of Troponin C, inducing conformational changes in Troponin C and the troponin complex. This process releases the inhibition of myosin-actin interaction, activates myosin ATPase, and facilitates cross-bridge cycling, ultimately generating myosin power strokes and muscle contraction. To date, no high-resolution structure of ssTnI has been determined. However, as homologous proteins, ssTnI, fast skeletal muscle Troponin I, and cardiac Troponin I share highly conserved structures. High-resolution crystallographic structures of partial cardiac and fast skeletal troponin complexes are available, and the structure-function relationship of ssTnI is inferred from studies on these related isoforms. Post-Translational Modifications No post-translational modifications of ssTnI have been identified to date. Mutations No human diseases have been reported to date as being associated with mutations in the TNNI1 gene. Clinical Significance The switch from slow to fast skeletal Troponin I isoforms serves as an indicator of slow-to-fast fiber type transitions during muscle adaptations. Slow skeletal Troponin I has been proposed as a sensitive and muscle fiber type-specific marker for skeletal muscle injuries. In patients with skeletal muscle disorders, intact ssTnI or its degraded products may be detected in peripheral blood, serving as a diagnostic indicator of slow fiber damage.
